q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE purpose of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) when it was founded in 1949.
parts.b: Explain ONE reason why the Soviet Union created the Warsaw Pact in 1955, using the historian's interpretation in the passage.
parts.c: Explain ONE way in which the alliance systems in Europe differed from earlier alliance systems such as those before 1914.

sample_answers.a: NATO was founded to provide collective defense against Soviet expansion: an attack on one member would be treated as an attack on all, deterring Soviet aggression in Western Europe.
sample_answers.b: According to the passage, the Soviet Union created the Warsaw Pact as a direct response to West Germany's admission into NATO, formalizing its control over Eastern European militaries and matching the Western alliance bloc for bloc.
sample_answers.c: Unlike the pre-1914 alliances, which were secretive bilateral deals among shifting partners, the Cold War blocs were permanent peacetime institutions with integrated military commands, standing forces, and an ideological dimension that divided the world into two camps.

q1.stimulus:
Historians describe the Cold War alliance systems as unprecedented: permanent, peacetime military blocs that divided Europe for four decades. NATO, founded in 1949, committed the United States to the defense of Western Europe — a revolutionary departure from America's traditional avoidance of entangling alliances. The Soviet Union answered with the Warsaw Pact in 1955, but historians stress an asymmetry: NATO was a genuine alliance of (mostly) sovereign states, while the Warsaw Pact was primarily an instrument for Soviet control over Eastern Europe, as the invasions of Hungary (1956) and Czechoslovakia (1968) demonstrated. Both alliances, however, served the same Cold War logic: each superpower used its bloc to organize its sphere, deter the rival, and prevent any member from defecting to the other side.
—Historian's account of Cold War alliances in the period c. 1900–present

q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE policy Truman announces in the doctrine.
parts.b: Describe ONE way in which the Truman Doctrine changed American foreign policy.
parts.c: Explain ONE reason why Truman framed the doctrine in universal terms rather than mentioning specific countries.

sample_answers.a: Truman announces that the United States will support free peoples resisting subjugation by armed minorities or outside pressures — committing America to oppose communist expansion anywhere in the world.
sample_answers.b: It ended America's traditional peacetime avoidance of foreign commitments by establishing a permanent global role: the United States would intervene politically, economically, and militarily to contain communism.
sample_answers.c: By speaking of 'free peoples' everywhere rather than naming Greece and Turkey (the immediate cases), Truman created a doctrine flexible enough to justify future interventions in any region, winning broader congressional and public support.

q2.stimulus:
I believe that it must be the policy of the United States to support free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures. I believe that we must assist free peoples to work out their own destinies in their own way. I believe that our help should be primarily through economic and financial aid which is essential to economic stability and orderly political processes.
—President Harry Truman, address to Congress (Truman Doctrine), 12 March 1947

q3.directions: Use the map below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE pattern shown on the map regarding military alliances in Cold War Europe.
parts.b: Explain ONE reason why the alliance blocs were divided roughly along the line shown on the map.
parts.c: Explain ONE way in which the map's division of Europe changed after 1989.

sample_answers.a: Europe is split into two blocs: NATO members in the west (including West Germany) and Warsaw Pact members in the east (including East Germany), with a few neutral states (such as Austria, Sweden, and Finland) between or alongside them — the 'Iron Curtain' made visible.
sample_answers.b: The line followed the positions of the Allied armies at the end of World War II: the Soviet Union kept the Eastern European territories its armies had liberated (and occupied), while the Western Allies organized their zones into NATO.
sample_answers.c: After the Cold War, the Warsaw Pact dissolved and most of its former members — Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic, the Baltic states — joined NATO, moving the alliance's eastern boundary hundreds of miles toward Russia.

q3.stimulus: The map shows Cold War military alliances in Europe from 1949 to 1989: NATO members (the United States, Canada, Britain, France, West Germany, Italy, and others in Western Europe) in one color, Warsaw Pact members (the Soviet Union, East Germany, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, and Albania) in another, and neutral states (Ireland, Sweden, Finland, Austria, Switzerland, Yugoslavia) unaligned. The map illustrates the Iron Curtain dividing the continent.
